fetched_contents.text: Contact Dermatitis: Symptoms, Causes, Types & Treatments What does contact dermatitis look like? Symptoms of contact dermatitis include a rash on your skin that’s: * Red to purple or darker than your natural skin tone. * Swollen, hive-like or elevated from the skin surrounding it. * Bumpy with a small cluster of pimples or blisters. * Oozing fluid or pus. * Painful with a burning or stinging sensation. * Flaky or scaling. * Itchy. Scratching your rash could break open your skin and cause a wound. If this wound becomes infected, it will look red and crusty and may be painful or leak pus. Where on my body will I have symptoms of contact dermatitis? You can experience contact dermatitis anywhere that your skin came into contact with an allergen or irritant. The most common places that people experience symptoms include: * Face, neck and scalp. * Lips, eyelids and cheeks. * Hands, fingers and arms. * Genitals (penis, vaginal area and vulva). * Armpits. * Feet and legs. What causes contact dermatitis? Physical contact with an allergen or an irritant causes contact dermatitis. If your body doesn’t like something that touches your skin, your immune system responds. When you see your skin swell or become inflamed, that’s a sign that your white blood cells are responding to the allergen or irritant, which can cause an itchy rash. The rash may appear in minutes if it’s caused by an irritant, or may take hours or days to appear after exposure to an allergen. Allergic contact dermatitis causes The most common causes of allergic contact dermatitis include: * Plants or parts of a plant (botanicals), like poison ivy. * Skin care products with fragrances. * Metals, such as nickel. * Medications, including antibiotics. * Preservatives or chemicals. Irritant contact dermatitis causes The most common causes of irritant contact dermatitis include: * Acids. * Cleaning products. * Body fluids, including urine and saliva. * Plants, like poinsettias and peppers. * Hair dyes. * Nail polish remover or other solvents. * Paints and varnishes. * Soaps or detergents. * Resins, plastics and epoxies. Is contact dermatitis contagious? If you encounter an allergen like poison ivy and touch someone else’s skin before you’ve washed yours, it’s possible to spread the allergen to them. They may then have a reaction if they’re also allergic. But contact dermatitis isn’t actually contagious. Your body’s reaction is unique to the material that touched it and not everyone reacts the same way. Can contact dermatitis spread? Depending on what caused your skin reaction, contact dermatitis can spread to other parts of your body. This is most common for allergic contact dermatitis. It happens when you touch an allergen and then touch other parts of your body before you realize that you’ve been in contact with it, or when multiple body parts touch the allergen and the reaction slowly unfolds in all areas of contact. If you notice your rash spreading to other parts of your body, contact a healthcare provider for treatment.

Immunological responses are due to the interaction of cytokines and T cells. In photo contact, allergic dermatitis lesions are confined to sun-exposed areas even though the allergen is in contact with covered areas. This activity reviews the causes, pathophysiology, and diagnosis of contact dermatitis and highlights the role of the interprofessional team in its management. Objectives: * Describe the causes of contact dermatitis. * Review the workup of a patient with contact dermatitis. * Summarize the treatment options for contact dermatitis. * Outline the importance of improving care coordination among interprofessional team members to improve outcomes for patients affected by contact dermatitis. Irritant contact dermatitis is a nonspecific response of the skin to direct chemical damage that releases mediators of inflammation predominantly from epidermal cells while allergic contact dermatitis is a delayed (type 4) hypersensitivity reaction to exogenous contact antigens. Immunological responses are due to the interaction of cytokines and T cells. In photo contact, allergic dermatitis lesions are confined to sun-exposed areas even though the allergen is in contact with covered areas. Until recently it was believed that allergic contact dermatitis was rare, unfortunately, data indicate that it is very common and affects close to 20% of children. The good news is that the majority of cases of contact dermatitis are self-limited and managed with simple supportive measures. However, in some patients, the disorder is chronic and can significantly affect the quality of life. Etiology Irritant contact dermatitis The likelihood of developing irritant contact dermatitis (irritant contact dermatitis ) increases with the duration, intensity, and concentration of the substance. Chemical or physical agents and microtrauma may produce skin irritation thus causing Irritant contact dermatitis. Physical irritants like friction, abrasions, occlusion, and detergents like sodium lauryl sulfate produce more irritant contact dermatitis in combination than alone.[5][6] The factors which determine the severity of irritant contact dermatitis include the quantity and concentration of the irritant, duration, and frequency of exposure. It also depends on the type of skin if it is thick, thin, oily, dry, very fair, previously damaged skin, or having a pre-existing atopic tendency. Environmental factors like high or low temperature and humidity also determine the severity. Studies have shown that washing with regular soap, e.g. Dial, is sufficient and should be done within a 2-hour window.[8] If the patient has not removed the urushiol oil from their skin within the appropriate time frame, high-potency topical steroids may be used to reduce inflammation in early stages, i.e. within 12 hours of exposure.[9] It should be noted that low-potency topical steroids are of little use and even high-potency steroids do not significantly relieve symptoms once vesicles have formed.[9] Epidemiology Females, infants, elderly, and individuals with atopic tendencies are more susceptible to irritant contact dermatitis. It is reported that up to 80% of cases of occupational dermatitis are irritant contact dermatitis.[10] All individuals are at risk of developing allergic contact dermatitis. Risk factors for allergic contact dermatitis include age, occupation, and history of atopic dermatitis. Overall contact dermatitis is most common in people with red hair and fair skin. Women are more likely to develop contact dermatitis because of the use of jewelry and fragrances. ## Mini-report: What contact dermatitis is and how it happens

Contact dermatitis is basically a skin rash that happens when your skin touches something that irritates it or makes it allergic [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R3]. It is not a single thing: it can be caused by either an **irritant** (something that directly hurts the skin) or an **allergen** (something your body reacts to as if it were harmful) [N1-R2][N1-R3][N1-R4][N4-F4]. The result is usually an itchy, swollen rash, and sometimes blisters or redness [N1-F1][N1-R5].

### Why some people get it and others don’t
The main reason people get contact dermatitis is because **some people are sensitive or allergic to the substance they touched** [N4-F4]. For example, poison ivy is one of the most common causes of allergic contact dermatitis, and up to 50–70% of adults may be sensitive to it [N4-F4]. That means if you are sensitive and touch urushiol (the oil in poison ivy), your immune system reacts and causes a rash. If you are not sensitive, you may not get a reaction at all [N1-F1][N4-F4].

### How poison ivy fits into this condition
Poison ivy is a classic example of allergic contact dermatitis. The rash is caused by an **allergic reaction to urushiol**, which is in the leaves, stems, and roots of poison ivy, poison oak, and poison sumac [N2-R1][N2-F2][N5-R2]. Urushiol sticks to your skin, and if you are allergic, your body treats it as a foreign substance. The rash usually appears 12 to 48 hours after exposure and can last weeks [N2-F2]. Poison ivy is therefore not just a “plant irritant” in the ordinary sense; it is a specific allergen that causes a delayed immune response [N2-R2][N4-F4].

In short: contact dermatitis is a skin rash from something you touched, and poison ivy is one of the most common causes because it triggers an allergic reaction in many people [N1-R1][N2-R1][N4-F4].

## Mini-report: What to do now and when to worry

### Best first steps after exposure
The best first thing is to **wash the affected area right away** with soap and water [N1-F1][N2-F2]. That helps remove as much of the irritant or allergen as possible. The Cleveland Clinic notes that washing off urushiol can reduce your chances of getting a poison ivy rash [N2-F2]. You should wash the skin thoroughly and gently, then dry it well [N3-F3].

If the rash is mild, the next step is to **apply a topical corticosteroid cream** to reduce inflammation and itching [N1-F1][N3-R1][N3-R2]. Over-the-counter hydrocortisone cream is one option, and the Mayo Clinic recommends applying it 1 to 2 times a day for a few days [N3-F3]. You can also use **cool compresses**, **cool baths with oatmeal**, and **anti-itch creams** or **calamine lotion** [N3-F3]. Avoid scratching, trim your nails, and cover the area if you can’t stop itching [N3-F3].

### When symptoms are serious and need medical help
You should see a doctor if:
- the reaction is **severe or widespread**,
- the skin continues to **swell**,
- the rash affects your **eyes, mouth, or genitals**,
- blisters are **oozing pus**,
- you develop a **fever greater than 100°F (37.8°C)**,
- the rash **doesn’t get better within a few weeks**,
- you **inhaled smoke from burning poison ivy** and are having **difficulty breathing** [N1-F1][N2-F2].

If the rash is very large or widespread, your doctor may prescribe **stronger steroid creams** or even **oral steroids** or pills [N3-R4][N3-F3].

### How to avoid spreading the rash
Contact dermatitis is **not contagious**, but the **allergen can spread** if you touch contaminated objects or other parts of your body before washing [N1-F1][N2-F2]. So you should:
- wash your hands and skin immediately after exposure,
- avoid touching other parts of your body until the area is clean,
- clean contaminated clothing, tools, or pets,
- avoid scratching, because bacteria under your nails can cause infection [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F3].

In short: wash right away, use a corticosteroid cream, and see a doctor if the rash is severe, spreading, or not improving [N1-F1][N3-F3][N2-F2].

## Mini-report: How to tell if the rash is poison ivy or another irritant

### Main features that point to poison ivy
The key features of a poison ivy rash are:
- **redness**, **itching**, **swelling**, and **blisters** [N2-F2][N1-F1],
- a **delayed reaction** that usually starts 12 to 48 hours after exposure [N2-F2],
- a rash that may appear in a **straight line** because the plant brushes against your skin, or more widely if you touch contaminated objects [N2-F2],
- **urushiol** as the cause, which is the oily resin in poison ivy, poison oak, and poison sumac [N2-R1][N2-F2][N5-R2].

Poison ivy is also one of the most common causes of **allergic contact dermatitis**, and many people are allergic to it [N4-F4].

### How to distinguish from other plant irritants
Other plant irritants may look similar, but they are usually caused by **physical irritation** rather than an allergic reaction. For example, poison ivy is allergic contact dermatitis, whereas some plant irritants can cause **direct irritation** from chemicals or oils [N1-R2][N1-R4][N1-F1]. The main difference is:
- **Allergic contact dermatitis** is a delayed immune reaction and can spread to other body parts even if you touch the allergen later [N1-F1][N4-F4],
- **Irritant contact dermatitis** is a direct skin reaction and often appears faster after contact [N1-R2][N1-R4].

Also, poison ivy is usually linked to **three-leaf plants** and **urushiol-containing plants** like poison oak and poison sumac, while other plant irritants may not have that same allergen [N2-F2][N5-R2].

### What the patient’s weed description suggests
The patient described **weeds with three leaves and shiny surfaces** [N1-F1]. That is a strong clue that poison ivy may be involved, because poison ivy is commonly described as having **three leaflets** [N2-F2][N5-R1][N5-R2]. However, **not every weed with three leaves is poison ivy**, and **not all poison ivy plants look the same** [N2-F2][N5-R3].

In short: the patient’s description points toward **poison ivy or a similar urushiol-containing plant**, but the rash could also be from another irritant or allergen [N2-F2][N5-R1][N5-R2]. The best way to tell is by looking at the **plant itself** and how the rash appears, and by washing the skin and avoiding further contact [N2-F2][N1-F1].

The best first thing is to **wash the affected area right away** with soap and water [N1-F1][N2-F2]. That helps remove as much of the irritant or allergen as possible. The best first thing is to **wash the affected area right away** with soap and water [N1-F1][N2-F2]. That helps remove as much of the irritant or allergen as possible. So the patient’s description points toward **poison ivy or a similar urushiol-containing plant**, but it is not a certainty [N2-F2][N5-R1][N5-R2]. The rash could also be from another irritant or allergen [N4-F4].

## What to do now

### Best first steps after exposure

The best first thing is to **wash the affected area right away** with soap and water [N1-F1][N2-F2]. That helps remove as much of the irritant or allergen as possible [N2-F2]. Wash thoroughly and gently, then dry well [N3-F3].

### What to use afterward

If the rash is mild, apply a **topical corticosteroid cream** to reduce inflammation and itching [N1-F1][N3-R1][N3-R2]. Over-the-counter hydrocortisone cream is one option, and the Mayo Clinic recommends using it 1 to 2 times a day for a few days [N3-F3]. You can also use **cool compresses**, **cool baths with oatmeal**, and **anti-itch creams** or **calamine lotion** [N3-F3].

### Avoid scratching

Do **not scratch** the rash, because scratching can make it worse and may even lead to infection [N1-F1][N3-F3]. Trim your nails and cover the area if needed [N3-F3].

## When to worry and when to see a doctor

You should see a doctor if:
- the reaction is **severe or widespread**,
- the skin continues to **swell**,
- the rash affects your **eyes, mouth, or genitals**,
- blisters are **oozing pus**,
- you develop a **fever greater than 100°F (37.8°C)**,
- the rash **doesn’t get better within a few weeks**,
- you **inhaled smoke from burning poison ivy** and are having **difficulty breathing** [N1-F1][N2-F2].

If the rash is very large or widespread, your doctor may prescribe **stronger steroid creams** or even **oral steroids** or pills [N3-R4][N3-F3].

## How to avoid spreading the rash

Contact dermatitis is **not contagious**, but the **allergen can spread** if you touch contaminated objects or other parts of your body before washing [N1-F1][N2-F2]. So you should:
- wash your hands and skin immediately after exposure,
- avoid touching other parts of your body until the area is clean,
- clean contaminated clothing, tools, or pets,
- avoid scratching, because bacteria under your nails can cause infection [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F3].

## Quick summary

- Contact dermatitis is a skin rash caused by something you touched that irritates it or makes it allergic [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R3].
- There are two main types: irritant contact dermatitis and allergic contact dermatitis [N1-R2][N1-R4][N4-F4].
- Poison ivy is a classic example of allergic contact dermatitis, and many people are allergic to it [N2-R2][N4-F4].
- The patient’s description of **three leaves and shiny surfaces** is a strong clue for poison ivy, but not a guarantee [N2-F2][N5-R1][N5-R2].
- The best first steps are to **wash right away** and use a **corticosteroid cream** [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F3].
- See a doctor if the rash is severe, spreading, or not improving [N1-F1][N2-F2].

So, in simple terms: your skin is reacting to something you touched — and the best bet is to wash, cool, and use a cream, then seek help if it gets worse [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F3].
